content: The following studies and findings provide insights into the management, treatment, and outcomes of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and related conditions: 1. Carosi et al. (2009) highlighted the risk of hepatitis B relapse in HBeAg-negative CHB patients who discontinued successful entecavir therapy, emphasizing the potential need for continuous antiviral treatment. 2. Kim et al. (2013) evaluated the durability of response after stopping nucleos(t)ide therapy in HBeAg-negative CHB patients, providing evidence on long-term outcomes. 3. Reijnders et al. (2010) demonstrated that nucleos(t)ide analogues often induce only temporary HBeAg seroconversion in most CHB patients, suggesting the need for ongoing monitoring. 4. Song et al. (2012) examined the durability of viral response after treatment cessation in HBeAg-positive CHB patients, offering insights into post-treatment management. 5. Chaung et al. (2012) reported a high frequency of recurrent viremia after HBeAg seroconversion and consolidation therapy, underscoring the importance of vigilant follow-up. 6. Fung et al. (2005) described the association of adefovir resistance with viral rebound and hepatic decompensation, highlighting the clinical implications of antiviral resistance. 7. Fontana et al. (2002) identified determinants of early mortality in patients with decompensated CHB treated with antiviral therapy, providing guidance for risk stratification. 8. Chien et al. (2003) explored the effects of lamivudine therapy on hepatic decompensation during acute exacerbations of CHB, demonstrating its potential benefits. 9. Lim et al. (2002) documented fatal hepatitis B reactivation following the discontinuation of nucleoside analogues, emphasizing the risks of treatment interruption. 10. Prati et al. (2002) updated the definitions of healthy ranges for serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, aiding in the interpretation of liver function tests. 11. Andersson and Chung (2009) reviewed monitoring strategies during and after antiviral therapy for hepatitis B, providing practical recommendations for clinical practice. 12. Chu and Liaw (2007) identified predictive factors for hepatitis B reactivation following HBeAg seroconversion, aiding in patient risk assessment. 13. Brunetto et al. (2010) demonstrated that hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels can help distinguish active from inactive HBV genotype D carriers, improving diagnostic accuracy. 14. Liang et al. (2012) compared entecavir and lamivudine for CHB treatment in a systematic review, highlighting the superior efficacy of entecavir. 15. Liu et al. (2014) conducted a meta-analysis comparing telbivudine and entecavir for nucleos(t)ide-naïve HBeAg-positive CHB patients, providing evidence for treatment selection. 16. Su and Ye (2012) analyzed the effects of telbivudine and entecavir in HBeAg-positive CHB patients, further supporting the efficacy of these agents. 17. Ye and Su (2013) performed a meta-analysis comparing entecavir and lamivudine in patients with hepatitis B-related decompensated cirrhosis, demonstrating the advantages of entecavir. 18. Heo et al. (2012) conducted a 96-week randomized trial on switching to entecavir in CHB patients with partial virological response to lamivudine, showing improved outcomes. 19. Hyun et al. (2012) compared the efficacy of lamivudine versus entecavir in patients with HBV-related decompensated cirrhosis, favoring entecavir for better clinical outcomes. 20. Bang et al. (2013) described the clinical course of patients with insufficient viral suppression during entecavir therapy in genotype C CHB, emphasizing the need for alternative strategies. 21. Hass et al. (2009) identified a rapid HBV DNA decrease at week 12 as a prognostic factor for first-line adefovir treatment in CHB, aiding in early treatment evaluation. 22. Reijnders et al. (2009) demonstrated that virologic response to adefovir therapy in CHB can be assessed at 24 weeks, providing a timeline for treatment monitoring. 23. McMahon et al. (2014) explored the relationship between HBV DNA levels and liver disease in a population-based study of HBeAg-negative individuals, highlighting the importance of viral load in disease progression. 24. Tohme et al. (2013) identified rates and risk factors for hepatitis B reactivation in inactive CHB carriers, providing insights into long-term management. 25. Papatheodoridis et al. (2012) reviewed follow-up and liver biopsy indications in HBeAg-negative CHB patients with persistently normal ALT, offering guidance for clinical decision-making. 26. Tai et al. (2009) examined the long-term outcomes of HBeAg-negative CHB carriers in relation to ALT changes, providing evidence for disease monitoring. 27. Feld et al. (2007) developed HBV DNA prediction rules for HBeAg-negative CHB, aiding in risk stratification and treatment planning. 28. The WHO (2013) consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention, emphasizing a public health approach. 29. Fernandez-Fernandez et al. (2011) updated the understanding of tenofovir nephrotoxicity, highlighting its clinical implications. 30. Rule (2007) discussed the implications of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) for identifying chronic kidney disease, aiding in renal function assessment. 31. Rodriguez-Nova et al. (2010) reviewed renal toxicity associated with tenofovir use, emphasizing the need for monitoring in clinical practice. 32. Sax et al. (2007) evaluated the renal safety of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, providing evidence for its use in HIV-infected patients. 33. Mateo et al. (2014) described hypophosphatemic osteomalacia induced by tenofovir in HIV-infected patients, highlighting a rare but significant adverse effect. 34. Bedimo et al. 35. Brown et al. (2009) reported bone mineral density loss after initiating antiretroviral therapy, independent of the regimen used. 36. Gallant et al. (2004) demonstrated the efficacy and safety of tenofovir DF versus stavudine in combination therapy for antiretroviral-naïve patients, favoring tenofovir. 37. Pradat et al. (2013) examined the evolution of eGFR in HIV-HBV co-infected patients receiving tenofovir, providing insights into renal outcomes. 38. Scherzer et al. 39. Tourret et al. (2013) discussed the dual effects of tenofovir on the kidneys of HIV-infected patients, highlighting its benefits and risks. 40. Pushpakom et al. (2011) identified genetic variants associated with tenofovir-induced kidney tubular dysfunction, providing insights into personalized medicine. 41. Yoshino et al. (2012) assessed renal function recovery after discontinuing tenofovir, demonstrating reversibility in some cases. 42. Mocroft et al. (2012) identified HBV and HCV co-infection as independent predictors of progressive kidney disease in HIV-positive adults, emphasizing the need for comprehensive care. 43. Petersen et al. (2013) reported the effectiveness of tenofovir for CHB in real-world practice, with interim results from a German multicenter study. 44. Heathcote et al. (2011) demonstrated the long-term efficacy and safety of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for CHB, supporting its use in clinical practice. 45. Lampertico et al. (2012) reported the 2-year effectiveness and safety of tenofovir in NUC-naïve CHB patients in a European multicenter study. 46. Marcellin et al. (2013) showed regression of cirrhosis during tenofovir treatment for CHB, with sustained benefits over five years. 47. Liaw et al. (2011) compared tenofovir, emtricitabine/tenofovir, and entecavir in patients with decompensated CHB liver disease, providing evidence for treatment selection. 48. Pan et al. (2014) evaluated the efficacy and safety of tenofovir in Asian-Americans with CHB, demonstrating its effectiveness in community settings. 49. de Vries-Sluijs et al. (2010) confirmed the long-term efficacy of tenofovir in HIV-HBV co-infected patients, supporting its use in co-infection management. 50. Stohr et al. (2011) identified risk factors for glomerular dysfunction following antiretroviral therapy initiation in Africa, emphasizing the need for renal monitoring. 51. Seto et al. (2013) described patterns of HBsAg decline and HBV DNA suppression in Asian CHB patients after three years of tenofovir treatment, providing insights into treatment outcomes. 52. Chang et al. (2010) demonstrated that long-term entecavir therapy results in fibrosis/cirrhosis reversal and continued histological improvement in CHB patients. 53. Tenney et al. (2009) reported that HBV resistance to entecavir in nucleoside-naïve patients is rare through five years of therapy, supporting its long-term use. 54. Wong et al. (2013) evaluated the accuracy of risk scores for CHB patients receiving entecavir treatment, aiding in clinical decision-making. 55. Hosaka et al. (2013) showed that long-term entecavir treatment reduces hepatocellular carcinoma incidence in CHB patients, highlighting its preventive benefits. 56. Yokosuka et al. (2010) reported the long-term use of entecavir in nucleoside-naïve Japanese CHB patients, demonstrating sustained efficacy. 57. Yuen et al. (2011) confirmed the safety and efficacy of three years of continuous entecavir therapy in treatment-naïve CHB patients. 58. Seto et al. (2014) described changes in HBsAg and HBV DNA levels in Chinese CHB patients after five years of entecavir treatment, providing evidence for its long-term benefits. 59. Lok et al. (2011) compared entecavir monotherapy to combination therapy with entecavir and tenofovir in nucleos(t)ide-naïve CHB patients, showing comparable outcomes. 60. Naicker (2003) discussed end-stage renal disease in sub-Saharan and South Africa, highlighting regional challenges in kidney disease management. 61. Murray et al. (2012) conducted a randomized trial of tenofovir in adolescents with CHB, demonstrating its efficacy and safety in this population. 62. Bonjoch et al. (2012) reported a high rate of reversibility of renal damage in HIV-infected patients receiving tenofovir-containing therapy, emphasizing the potential for recovery. 63. WHO (2013) provided consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention, emphasizing a public health approach. 64. Lozano et al. (2012) analyzed global and regional mortality from various causes, including liver disease, providing a comprehensive overview of disease burden. 65. Zhang et al. (2004) conducted a randomized trial of hepatocellular carcinoma screening, demonstrating its impact on early detection and outcomes. 66. Chen et al. (2003) reported the results of a randomized trial on liver cancer screening in Qidong, China, highlighting the benefits of surveillance. 67. Yang et al. (1999) conducted a prospective study on secondary prevention for primary liver cancer, providing evidence for early intervention. 68. Yang et al. (1996) evaluated early detection methods for primary liver cancer, emphasizing the importance of timely diagnosis. 69. Yang et al. (1997) conducted a prospective study on early detection for primary liver cancer, demonstrating the benefits of surveillance. 70. Zhang and Yang (2001) evaluated liver cancer surveillance in high-risk populations in Shanghai, providing evidence for targeted screening. 71. Han et al. (2013) showed that hepatocellular carcinoma survival improves with surveillance intervals of six months or less, compared to longer intervals. 72. Kim et al. (2007) demonstrated that semiannual surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma improves survival compared to annual surveillance. 73. Sherman et al. (1995) evaluated hepatocellular carcinoma screening in chronic HBV carriers, providing insights into incidence and prevalence. 74. Gounder (2010) compared the cost of hepatocellular carcinoma screening using ultrasound alone versus a two-step approach with alpha-fetoprotein, providing cost-effectiveness data. 75. Romero (2010) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of a clinical pathway for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance in Colombia, emphasizing economic considerations. 76. Coon (2007) conducted a systematic review and economic analysis of cirrhosis surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma, providing evidence for cost-effective strategies. 77. Aghoram et al. (2012) reviewed the use of alpha-fetoprotein and/or liver ultrasonography for hepatocellular carcinoma screening in CHB patients, providing updated recommendations. 78. McMahon et al. (2000) conducted a 16-year population-based study on hepatocellular carcinoma screening in Alaska natives with CHB, demonstrating the benefits of long-term surveillance. 79. Kansagara et al. (2014) conducted a systematic review of hepatocellular carcinoma screening in chronic liver disease, providing evidence for its effectiveness. 80. Tong et al. (2010) demonstrated that hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance improves survival in Asian-American CHB patients, emphasizing the importance of community-based programs. 81. Yu et al. (2004) evaluated the impact of ultrasonography-based surveillance on hepatocellular carcinoma prognosis, demonstrating improved outcomes. 82. Chen et al. (2010) reported that inactive HBV carriers remain at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma and liver-related death, emphasizing the need for ongoing monitoring. 83. Chen et al. (2011) demonstrated that changes in serum HBV DNA and ALT levels determine the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, providing evidence for dynamic risk assessment. 84. Chen and Yang (2011) reviewed the natural history of CHB, providing insights into disease progression and management. 85. Chen et al. (2006) demonstrated that serum HBV DNA levels are a key determinant of hepatocellular carcinoma risk, emphasizing the importance of viral load monitoring. 86. Loomba et al. (2013) reported the synergistic effects of family history and HBV infection on hepatocellular carcinoma risk, highlighting the importance of genetic and viral factors. 87. Nakazawa et al. (2011) identified viral load as an indicator of long-term outcomes in HBeAg-negative CHB carriers with normal ALT levels, providing evidence for risk stratification. 88. Papatheodoridis et al. (2008) described longitudinal changes in serum HBV DNA levels and predictors of progression in HBeAg-negative CHB, aiding in disease monitoring. 89. Wong and Wong (2013) reviewed risk prediction for HBV-related hepatocellular carcinoma in the era of antiviral therapy, providing updated insights. 90. Tai et al. (2009) examined the long-term outcomes of HBeAg-negative CHB carriers in relation to ALT changes, providing evidence for disease monitoring. 91. Yuen et al. (2005) identified prognostic determinants for CHB in Asians, providing therapeutic implications for clinical practice. 92. Ribes et al. (2006) identified cofactors associated with liver disease mortality in an HBsAg-positive Mediterranean cohort, providing insights into long-term outcomes. 93. Seo et al. (2014) reported that the coexistence of HBsAg and anti-HBs may increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in CHB patients, emphasizing the need for careful monitoring. 94. Hann et al. (2012) demonstrated the predictive value of alpha-fetoprotein for long-term hepatocellular carcinoma risk in CHB patients, providing evidence for its use in surveillance. 95. Yang et al. (2011) evaluated liver-associated morbidity and mortality in HIV-HBV co-infected Chinese patients, providing insights into co-infection management. 96. Shimakawa et al. (2013) associated early age at CHB establishment with persistent viral replication, liver cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, emphasizing the importance of early intervention. 97. Yang et al. (2011) developed and validated a predictive score for hepatocellular carcinoma risk in CHB patients, aiding in clinical decision-making. 98. Yuen et al. (2009) identified independent risk factors and a predictive score for hepatocellular carcinoma development in CHB, providing evidence for risk stratification. 99. Wong et al. (2010) developed a clinical scoring system to predict hepatocellular carcinoma in CHB carriers, aiding in risk assessment. 100. Sherman (2013) reviewed the impact of hepatitis B treatment on hepatocellular carcinoma incidence, providing evidence for its preventive benefits. 101. WHO (2009) emphasized the importance of hepatitis B vaccination in reducing disease burden, highlighting its role in prevention. 102. Dumolard (2008) reported on the global implementation of newborn hepatitis B vaccination, demonstrating its impact on disease prevention. 103. Levin et al. (2005) analyzed the costs of delivering a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine in Indonesia, providing evidence for cost-effective strategies. 104. Goldstein et al. (2005) developed a mathematical model to estimate the global hepatitis B disease burden and vaccination impact, providing insights into public health planning. 105. Margolis et al. (1995) conducted an economic analysis of hepatitis B immunization, demonstrating its cost-effectiveness in preventing disease transmission. 106. Beasley et al. (1983) demonstrated the efficacy of hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine in preventing perinatal HBV transmission, providing evidence for its use in maternal and neonatal care. 107. Chen (2010) emphasized the importance of hepatitis B vaccination in eliminating and eradicating HBV infection, highlighting its public health significance. 108. Chen (2009) reviewed the role of hepatitis B vaccination in achieving elimination and eradication goals, providing evidence for its global impact. 109. del Canho et al. (1997) reported on the long-term efficacy and immunogenicity of neonatal hepatitis B vaccination in the Netherlands, demonstrating its protective benefits. 110. Xu et al. (2002) identified risk factors and mechanisms of transplacental HBV transmission, providing insights into maternal-fetal care. 111. Li et al. (2003) conducted a clinical study on interrupting HBV intrauterine transmission, demonstrating the effectiveness of preventive strategies. 112. van Zonneveld et al. (2003) evaluated lamivudine treatment during pregnancy to prevent perinatal HBV transmission, providing evidence for its use in maternal care. 113. Burk et al. (1994) demonstrated that maternal HBV viral load influences perinatal transmission outcomes, emphasizing the importance of viral load monitoring. 114. Mandelbrot et al. (2001) evaluated the combination of lamivudine and zidovudine for preventing maternal-infant HIV transmission, providing evidence for combination therapy. 115. Xu et al. (2009) conducted a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study on lamivudine use in late pregnancy to prevent perinatal HBV transmission, demonstrating its efficacy. 116. Yang et al. (2013) reviewed the effects of high viral hepatitis B levels, providing insights into disease management.
